findings.title: installation_id is saved before OAuth state is validated
findings.body: OAuthLoginView writes installation_id into the pipeline with bind_state before it checks that state matches pipeline.signature and before the authorization code is exchanged. bind_state persists the session immediately, and PipelineAdvancerView leaves csrf_protect = False, so a cross-site GET to /extensions/github/setup/?installation_id=<attacker> overwrites an in-progress install even when state is missing or wrong and the view then returns the error page. The later legitimate OAuth callback usually has no installation_id, and GitHubInstallation falls back to that poisoned value (request.GET.get("installation_id", pipeline.fetch_state("installation_id"))). The victim's org is then attached to the attacker's GitHub App installation whenever the sender check is skipped, or their own install is broken if the check runs. Persist installation_id only after state validation succeeds, and do not update pipeline state on the failure path.

findings.title: User-match check skipped when Integration does not exist
findings.body: The new control is supposed to reject a mismatch between the OAuth GitHub login and the user who installed the app, but that comparison runs only after an Integration row is already loaded. On Integration.DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation returns pipeline.next_step() with no check. build_integration never reads github_authenticated_user; it fetches /app/installations/{id} with the GitHub App JWT, which can see every installation of this app, not only ones the OAuth user owns. Webhook creation of the Integration races the browser redirect, and any installation whose Sentry row is missing or was deleted takes this path. Combined with installation_id coming from the query string, an attacker can link a chosen GitHub App installation to the current Sentry organization and inherit the app's access to that account's repositories. Fail closed unless the OAuth user is verified against the installing user, or against installations visible to that user's token, before the org link is created.

findings.title: Token request drops redirect_uri sent on authorize
findings.body: The authorize redirect includes redirect_uri, but the access-token POST only sends code, client_id, and client_secret. GitHub's token endpoint, following RFC 6749 section 4.1.3, requires the same redirect_uri on the token request when it was included in authorization; otherwise it returns an error instead of access_token. This handler then always shows the invalid-installation page, so every install fails after the user authorizes, and that page is the same one used for real verification failures, so a manual check of the error UI does not prove the happy path. The comment says this mirrors OAuth2CallbackView.get_token_params, which includes redirect_uri. Tests stub the token URL and ignore the POST body, so they stay green. Send the same redirect_uri used in the authorize request, build that URL with urlencode (the current f-string leaves redirect_uri unencoded), and accept both form and JSON token bodies the way the shared callback view does.

findings.title: Missing sender crashes the re-link path
findings.body: The match check indexes integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] directly. Integrations created before sender was stored, or created by build_integration when pipeline state has no sender, have no sender object. That raises KeyError, or TypeError if sender is null, and the install 500s instead of rendering the installation-failed page. This is exactly the re-link branch (Integration exists, no OrganizationIntegration), so those records cannot be reinstalled. The inequality also does not require both values to be non-empty strings, so a null sender login and a missing github_authenticated_user would compare equal and be allowed through. Read sender with a safe lookup and deny unless both logins are present and equal.

findings.title: User-info fetch errors bypass the error page
findings.body: After the token exchange, get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) is called with no try/except. HTTP errors, network failures, and a non-mapping response propagate as an uncaught exception and a 500, unlike a missing access_token or a bad state, which return the installation-failed page. A GitHub /user failure during install therefore aborts opaquely, and the exception can capture the request that carries the new user access token into error reporting. Catch API failures and treat a missing login the same as the other verification failures.

findings.title: Security tests never reach the checks they describe
findings.body: test_installation_not_found used to assert "The GitHub installation could not be found." when the installation API returned 404. It now calls the callback with state ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which is not the pipeline signature 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3, so it fails the state check and never reaches build_integration. test_github_user_mismatch mutates the installation webhook body (installation id and sender login) but keeps HTTP_X_HUB_SIGNATURE sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486 from the original fixture, so signature verification rejects it when enabled, and then it reuses that same hardcoded state for a second user while asserting only the generic "Invalid installation request." string. That string is also returned for a state mismatch, a bad code, and a missing token, so the test can pass without comparing octocat to sender "attacker" or showing that no OrganizationIntegration was created. The token stub returns access_token regardless of redirect_uri. Recompute the webhook signature, drive a callback whose state actually matches that pipeline, and assert the specific denial for user mismatch, missing sender, and Integration.DoesNotExist.
